clue.text: Champion traps a wild animal

indicators.note: whatever traps something holds it inside itself, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to champion is to be the best
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sporting champion catches a ferocious creature.
explanation.walkthrough: BEST opens to hold A: BE(A)ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A beast is any animal, especially a large untamed or dangerous one.

clue.text: Different wire in separate rocket, say

indicators.note: a different version of the word means its letters come out in another order
one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: to fork is to split or divide, as a road does
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An electrician threads another wire through a separate model rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Separate' looks like an adjective but is the verb fork, split like a road; 'say' marks a rocket as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocket is one kind of pyrotechnic display item, launched into the sky to explode.

clue.text: Cushion regularly found under head of sleeper

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting under another means it follows it in the grid
the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: its first letter
something done regularly is done frequently

explanation.surface: A pillow is routinely placed beneath a sleeping person's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cushion' looks like a noun in the bedroom scene, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To cushion a blow is to make it less hard, lessen its impact.

clue.text: Brain left fool

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
an oaf is a clumsy, stupid person

explanation.surface: A clever person walked out on an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British slang for 'use your head', from the rhyming slang loaf of bread = head.
explanation.definitionFit: In British informal speech one's head or intelligence is called this, from cockney rhyming slang.

clue.text: Smashed, drunkard as he drinks bottles

indicators.note: to bottle something is to hold it inside, so the run of letters is contained within the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the next two words and the start of the last

explanation.surface: A drunk, plastered, keeps putting away bottles of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashed' and 'drunkard' make you think of being drunk, but the definition is about breaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopes that are dashed are shattered or destroyed, as a thing is when smashed against something hard.

clue.text: Infinite spring gone then?

parts.note: to spring is to leap or jump
the suffix meaning without, so the leap has gone

explanation.surface: A puzzled observer asks whether endless means the bounce has worn off.
explanation.walkthrough: Read cryptically, 'bound-less' is a state where the spring has gone; the question mark flags that playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without limits or edges is endless, having no end at all.

clue.text: Mark is cool with men on manoeuvres

indicators.note: troops on manoeuvres move about and change position, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these words, with IS from the link, rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier called Mark is relaxed among the troops during army exercises.
explanation.definitionFit: A semicolon is a punctuation symbol, a written sign on the page.

clue.text: Meat company in embargo

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: an embargo is an official ban on trade
CO is the usual abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A meat firm is caught up in a trade embargo.
explanation.walkthrough: BAN opens to take CO: BA(CO)N.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacon is cured pork from the back or sides of a pig.

clue.text: Sweet flirt toyed with emotions, initially

indicators.note: letters that are toyed with are played around with and shifted out of place

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A charming flirt played with someone's feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective for the flirt, but it is a noun for a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A trifle is a British layered dessert of sponge, fruit, custard and cream, a pudding.

clue.text: Uphill path, a track

parts.note: taken as written
the scent is the trail a hound follows when tracking

explanation.surface: A track climbing up a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' looks like part of the path picture, but here it is the trail an animal leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is a climb, or a route going up a slope.

clue.text: Old coin, item from a long way back?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a former British coin worth a quarter of a penny

definitions.text: item from a long way back?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: an object that is distant

explanation.surface: An antique coin is an object from long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the answer into FAR and THING; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The British farthing was a small copper coin, withdrawn in 1960; a 'far thing' is literally a distant object.

clue.text: Part of eye with ear, ear cut

indicators.note: a word that is cut is shortened, losing its final letter

parts.note: an ear of grain, so corn
taken as written, then shortened

explanation.surface: An eye part paired with an ear, the ear being cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'ear' is the head of a cereal plant, not the organ.
explanation.definitionFit: The cornea is the clear front layer covering the iris and pupil of the eyeball.

clue.text: Yorkshire river with last of water, drier

parts.note: the Aire flows through Leeds in Yorkshire

indicators.note: last of points to the closing letter of the word that follows

parts.note: its last letter

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire river runs low, with the water level dropping.
explanation.walkthrough: An airer is a clothes horse, a frame for drying washing, common in British homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothes airer is a rack used for drying laundry, so it is a drier.

clue.text: Toy, something played on

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to play idly with something, fidget
second meaning: a violin, which is played

explanation.walkthrough: 'Toy' looks like a noun for a plaything, but it is the verb, as in toying with your food.
explanation.definitionFit: To fiddle with something is to fidget with it; a fiddle is an informal name for the violin.

clue.text: Savage biting arm briefly suffered as if the victim?

indicators.note: a mouth biting something closes around it, holding it inside

parts.note: savage means fierce and violent

indicators.note: a word said briefly is cut short, losing its end

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened

explanation.surface: A wild beast's teeth sank into someone's arm.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase: feeling something second-hand, through another person's experience.
explanation.definitionFit: Vicarious feelings are experienced through another person, sharing their pain as though it were your own.

clue.text: Pot with lid off spilling coloured fluid

indicators.note: the lid is the top, so only the opening letter of the next word is taken off it

parts.note: its first letter
ink is a coloured liquid for writing

explanation.surface: A paint pot with its lid removed spills its contents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' looks like the container in the scene; it is the snooker verb, to send a ball into a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker or pool, to pot a ball is to send it into a pocket, so these verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Forcefully push boat

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to shove your way roughly
second meaning: a flat-bottomed river vessel

explanation.definitionFit: To barge in or past is to push rudely through; a barge is a long flat canal vessel.

clue.text: Shakespearean character, lowest part

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream
second meaning: the base of anything

explanation.definitionFit: Nick Bottom is the weaver given an ass's head in the play; the bottom of something is its base.

clue.text: Army in triumph, ostensibly

indicators.note: the run of letters sits inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: the last letter of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: A victorious army, or so it appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Host is an old word for a great multitude, especially an armed force, as in heavenly host.

clue.text: Other lip damaged where chopper may have come down?

definitions.text: where chopper may have come down?

indicators.note: something damaged is broken and knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's other lip got hurt where an axe or cleaver fell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' suggests a blade, but here it is slang for a helicopter.
explanation.definitionFit: A heliport is a landing site for helicopters, which are nicknamed choppers.

clue.text: Briton given master's degree — lucky thing?

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts
a Scot is a native of Scotland, a Briton

explanation.surface: A British student, newly awarded a master's degree, is fortunate.
explanation.walkthrough: The degree is written before the Briton even though the clue names it second.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or object thought to bring good fortune to a team.

clue.text: Rough, rocky ground in which article is buried

indicators.note: the rearranged word is the place another piece goes inside
something buried is hidden inside, enclosed by its surroundings
something ground is crushed and broken up, so the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper article lies buried under rough, stony earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A croaky voice is hoarse and harsh-sounding, as with a sore throat.

clue.text: Entertain girl in green, removing coat

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other
taking off a coat strips the outside layer, so the outer letters go

parts.note: taken as written, then stripped
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A girl dressed in green takes off her coat to put on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: Gal is an informal, chiefly American word for a girl; the coat is the colour word's first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To regale guests is to amuse or delight them, usually with stories or lavish hospitality.

clue.text: Language very similar, though not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means a word stops short, missing its final letter

parts.note: germane means closely related or relevant

explanation.surface: Two languages are almost but not quite alike.
explanation.walkthrough: Germane, meaning relevant, loses its last E.
explanation.definitionFit: German is the tongue spoken in Germany, Austria and much of Switzerland.

clue.text: Earliest tree on street

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece set on another stands above it, so it is written ahead

parts.note: a fir is a conifer
ST is the usual abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: The oldest tree growing on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: First means coming before all others in time, so the initial or soonest.

clue.text: Japanese dish I'm returning, nothing special, finished

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: the letters as written, apostrophe dropped
so-so means mediocre, nothing out of the ordinary
as in 'time is up'

explanation.surface: A diner says they are going back for an unremarkable Japanese meal, and have eaten it all.
explanation.walkthrough: MI from the reversal, then SO-SO and UP.
explanation.definitionFit: Miso soup is a Japanese broth made with fermented soybean paste, served with most meals.

clue.text: White stick

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a pointed wooden stake used in fencing

explanation.walkthrough: The words read as a white cane, but they are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale face is whitish and drained of colour; a pale is also a fence stake, as in beyond the pale.

clue.text: Concerned with couple put back together

parts.note: re means regarding, about
a couple is two, a pair

explanation.surface: Someone worried about a couple trying to reunite them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put back together' looks like the reconciled couple, but it is a verb for fixing something broken.
explanation.definitionFit: To repair something is to mend or fix it, restoring it to working condition.

clue.text: 20 Down dog?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the answer to 20 Down, a hoarse sort of voice
second meaning: an Arctic sled breed

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference supplies a meaning of rough and hoarse; the question mark marks the dog as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A husky voice sounds low and rasping like a croaky one; the husky is a sled-pulling breed from the Arctic.

clue.text: Flier over southern oceans, rare bird on course?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the great seabird of the Southern Hemisphere
second meaning: a golf score of three under par on a hole, rarer than an eagle

explanation.walkthrough: Golf names its under-par scores after birds; 'course' is the golf course, not a flight path.
explanation.definitionFit: The albatross is a huge ocean-going seabird; in golf it is a score of three strokes under par.
